items.followUp: Define reduction and give one example.

rubric.why: Identifies a standard definition of oxidation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that oxidation is loss of electrons or gain of oxygen.

rubric.why: A correct example shows oxidation occurring.
rubric.description: Gives a valid example of oxidation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct example, such as magnesium reacting with oxygen to form magnesium oxide.

modelAnswer: Oxidation is the loss of electrons by an atom or ion; it can also be described as the gain of oxygen.
For example: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO. Magnesium is oxidized by oxygen.

items.followUp: Why are platinum and gold called noble metals?

rubric.why: Their low tendency to lose electrons is the basis of their low reactivity.
rubric.description: States their low tendency to react or form positive ions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for saying that silver and gold have little tendency to lose electrons or form positive ions.

rubric.why: Links their low reactivity to the difficulty of removing electrons or oxidizing them.
rubric.description: Explains why their low reactivity occurs.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking this to high ionization energy or resistance to oxidation.

modelAnswer: Silver and gold have little tendency to lose electrons and form positive ions.
They therefore resist oxidation and are less reactive than most metals.

items.followUp: Why does potassium have a lower ionization energy than sodium?

rubric.why: Sodium's outer electron is nearer the nucleus than potassium's.
rubric.description: Compares the atomic sizes or shell structure of sodium and potassium.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that sodium has fewer electron shells or a smaller atomic radius.

rubric.why: The stronger attraction makes sodium's outer electron harder to remove.
rubric.description: Links the smaller size to the greater ionization energy of sodium.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that sodium's outer electron is more strongly attracted to the nucleus and requires more energy to remove.

modelAnswer: Sodium has fewer electron shells and a smaller atomic radius than potassium.
Its outermost electron is closer to the nucleus and is more strongly attracted, so more energy is needed to remove it.

rubric.why: Metallic character describes the electron-losing behaviour of metals.
rubric.description: Defines metallic character as the tendency to lose electrons and form cations.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for a complete definition; award 1 mark if only the tendency to lose electrons or form positive ions is stated.

modelAnswer: Metallic character is the tendency of an atom to lose electrons and form positive ions (cations).

items.followUp: Differentiate between cast iron and steel.

rubric.why: The composition distinguishes ordinary steel from stainless steel.
rubric.description: States the composition of steel and stainless steel.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying steel as an iron–carbon alloy and stainless steel as iron alloyed with chromium, often with nickel.

rubric.why: Chromium gives stainless steel its resistance to corrosion.
rubric.description: States the difference in corrosion resistance.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that ordinary steel can rust, whereas stainless steel resists corrosion.

modelAnswer: Steel is an alloy of iron and carbon; it can rust.
Stainless steel is an iron alloy containing chromium, often nickel as well, and resists corrosion.

items.followUp: Define an ion and describe the difference between a cation and an anion.

rubric.why: A molecule consists of atoms chemically joined and acting as one unit.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for defining a molecule as two or more chemically bonded atoms that behave as a unit.

rubric.why: These are two molecule types classified by the number of atoms per molecule.
rubric.description: Names and exemplifies monatomic and diatomic molecules.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for each type with a suitable example.

rubric.why: These are further types classified by the number of atoms per molecule.
rubric.description: Names and exemplifies triatomic and polyatomic molecules.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for each type with a suitable example.

modelAnswer: A molecule is a group of two or more atoms chemically bonded together and behaving as a single unit.
A monatomic molecule contains one atom, e.g. He.
A diatomic molecule contains two atoms, e.g. H₂.
A triatomic molecule contains three atoms, e.g. O₃.
A polyatomic molecule contains more than three atoms, e.g. P₄ or S₈.

items.followUp: Describe how protons were discovered and give two of their properties.

rubric.why: The beryllium experiment and the resulting evidence describe the discovery of the neutron.
rubric.description: Describes the discovery of the neutron.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying Chadwick and the 1932 experiment; award 1 mark for describing alpha-particle bombardment of beryllium and the neutral radiation that ejected protons from paraffin wax.

rubric.why: Zero electric charge is a defining neutron property.
rubric.description: States that a neutron has no charge.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that a neutron is electrically neutral.

rubric.why: A neutron has a mass close to that of a proton and is found in the nucleus.
rubric.description: States one further correct property of neutrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that its mass is approximately 1 amu or that it is present in the atomic nucleus.

modelAnswer: In 1932, James Chadwick bombarded beryllium with alpha particles.
A highly penetrating neutral radiation was produced; it knocked protons out of paraffin wax, leading Chadwick to identify the neutron.
A neutron has no electric charge.
Its mass is approximately 1 amu, and it is found in the atomic nucleus.

items.followUp: Define dipole-dipole forces and state how they affect boiling points.

rubric.why: Hydrogen bonding is the specific attraction involving hydrogen bonded to a highly electronegative atom.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for describing the attraction between H bonded to F, O, or N and a lone pair on an electronegative atom; award 1 mark for a partly correct definition.

rubric.why: Extra energy is needed to overcome hydrogen bonds between molecules.
rubric.description: Explains an effect on boiling point.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that hydrogen bonding raises boiling point because more energy is needed to separate molecules.

rubric.why: Hydrogen bonding also affects other physical properties of substances.
rubric.description: States another physical-property effect of hydrogen bonding.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct further effect, such as increased viscosity or surface tension, altered solubility, or ice being less dense than liquid water.

modelAnswer: Hydrogen bonding is the attraction between a hydrogen atom bonded to F, O, or N and a lone pair on an electronegative atom in the same or a neighbouring molecule.
Hydrogen bonds increase intermolecular attraction, so more energy is needed to separate molecules and the boiling point is raised.
They also affect properties such as viscosity, surface tension, and solubility; in water, hydrogen bonding makes ice less dense than liquid water.
